summary: This informational RFC describes MIKEY-SAKKE, a key exchange method for Multimedia Internet KEYing. It uses identity-based public key cryptography to establish a shared secret and certificateless signatures to authenticate the source. Its stated features include scalability, low-latency call setup, and simplex transmission.

plainLanguage.summary: Two people starting a secure call need to agree on a secret code. This method lets them do it using just their names, quickly, so the call can start right away.

questions: identity based key exchange for secure calls
subtitle: Identity-based key exchange for multimedia calls with built-in source authentication.

tldr.problem: Multimedia systems need to establish shared secrets quickly for secure calls, but traditional methods require complex certificate infrastructure and slow handshakes.
tldr.mechanism: MIKEY-SAKKE uses identity-based public-key cryptography where public keys are derived from identities (like phone numbers), eliminating the need for certificates. A trusted Key Management Service distributes secret keys periodically, allowing two parties to exchange keys in a single transmission.
tldr.outcome: Devices can establish secure calls with low latency (half a roundtrip), scalability without constant KMS availability, and support for features like call forwarding and secure voicemail.

today: RFC 6509 is an Informational specification published in February 2012. It remains the definition of MIKEY-SAKKE and has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Overview of MIKEY-SAKKE
sections.content:
MIKEY-SAKKE is a key exchange method built on MIKEY (Multimedia Internet KEYing), a framework for distributing encryption keys to secure real-time communication. Unlike earlier MIKEY modes that use RSA or Diffie-Hellman, MIKEY-SAKKE uses Identity-Based Public Key Cryptography (IDPKC), where a person's public key is derived from their identity (such as a phone number) rather than from a separate certificate.

The method uses SAKKE (Sakai-Kasahara Key Encryption) for the key exchange and ECCSI (Elliptic Curve-based Certificateless Signatures) for authentication. A trusted Key Management Service (KMS) acts as the root of trust: it generates and distributes secret keys to users periodically, but does not need to be online during actual communication.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of needing a certificate server to prove who you are, you and the KMS agree on a secret based on your name. The KMS gives you a special key once a month, and you can use it to talk securely to anyone without asking the KMS for help.

sections.title: The Key Exchange Process
sections.content:
The exchange happens in a single message from the Initiator (the person starting the call) to the Responder (the person receiving the call). The Initiator sends an I_MESSAGE containing four key parts: a header with a random session ID, a random value (RAND) used to derive session keys, SAKKE Encapsulated Data (the encrypted shared secret), and a digital signature to prove the Initiator's identity.

The Responder receives this message, validates the signature using the Initiator's public identity, and then decrypts the SAKKE data using its own secret key to recover the shared secret value (SSV). This SSV becomes the TGK (TEK Generation Key), from which all session keys are derived. No response message is needed because both parties are mutually authenticated after processing the single message.
sections.plainLanguage: The caller sends a package with a locked box containing a secret. The receiver uses their special key to unlock it. If the box is really from who it claims to be and opens correctly, the receiver knows it's safe.

sections.title: Identities and Key Periods
sections.content:
Identifiers in MIKEY-SAKKE are constructed from two elements: a timestamp (year and month, like "2012-02") and a constrained telephone URI (a phone number in the form tel:+447700900123). For example, a user's Identifier might be the ASCII string 2012-02\0tel:+447700900123\0.

The timestamp enforces key period changes. Keys are updated regularly (typically monthly) to limit the damage from device compromise: if a device is stolen and reported, it can eavesdrop on calls only for the remainder of the current month. Implementations hold two periods' keys simultaneously to handle clock differences between devices. This design eliminates the need for real-time certificate revocation mechanisms.
sections.plainLanguage: Your identity includes the month, like "February - your phone number." When March starts, you get new keys from the KMS, and your old keys stop working. If someone steals your phone in February, they can only eavesdrop until the end of the month.

sections.title: Message Structure and Payloads
sections.content:
An I_MESSAGE contains several payloads defined in the MIKEY framework. The Common Header (HDR) includes a randomly chosen Crypto Session Bundle ID and a V bit (set to 0 to indicate no response is expected). The Timestamp payload (using NTP format) allows the Responder to determine which key period is in use. Optional IDR payloads identify the Initiator, Responder, and their respective KMSs.

The SAKKE payload contains the encapsulated data formatted as defined in RFC 6508, with fields indicating which SAKKE parameter set and identifier scheme are in use. The SIGN payload holds the signature; ECCSI signatures are recommended (signature type 2), but RSA signatures (types 0 or 1) with certificates are also allowed. Optional security policy payloads indicate which encryption and authentication algorithms the Initiator supports.
sections.plainLanguage: The message is a package with a label (header) showing when it was sent, an locked box (SAKKE payload) with the secret inside, and a signature proving it came from the right person.

sections.title: Forking, Groups, and Deferred Delivery
sections.content:
MIKEY-SAKKE supports multiple use cases beyond simple unicast calls. In forking, a user's Receiver Secret Key is loaded on multiple devices (e.g., a desk phone and a mobile), so incoming calls can be handled by any device. Each device should have a different Secret Signing Key for the same identity, which ECCSI allows.

For group calls, the Initiator forms one I_MESSAGE per group member, all using the same shared secret. A conference bridge can also initiate the call and distribute the SSV to group members. In deferred delivery (voicemail), a server stores the I_MESSAGE along with encrypted content. When the recipient requests the message, the server forwards the stored I_MESSAGE, and the recipient decrypts using the key material from that period. The deferred delivery server does not need to implement MIKEY-SAKKE itself, only store and forward the messages.
sections.plainLanguage: You can send the same secret box to multiple friends (group), let your voicemail server save secret boxes and play them back later (deferred delivery), or have your office and mobile phone both listen for incoming calls (forking).
